data.title: Ecommerce earnings recap: Macy's, Signet Jewelers, Reformation and more
data.description:
Some of the largest online retailers in North America have reported their ecommerce earnings results over the past week.

Parentheses indicate the merchant’s ranking in the Top 2000 Database, if applicable. Retailers are in alphabetical order. The market research tool ranks North America’s largest ecommerce retailers by their annual web sales.

Ecommerce earnings results for the week ending Sept. 11

Academy Sports and Outdoors (No. 142)

In its fiscal Q2 2026, Academy Sports and Outdoors ecommerce sales increased 12.8% year over year. That was more than quadruple the growth rate of its total sales, at 3%, which rose to $1.6 billion. Meanwhile, comparable sales decreased 0.4% year over year, indicating ecommerce’s role in Academy Sports and Outdoors’ fiscal Q2.

Chief financial officer Earl Ford noted that Academy Sports and Outdoors has continued investing in its ecommerce channel, calling it a strength on the retailer’s earnings call. He said the retailer has been investing both in ecommerce technology and in customer data.

For the first half of its fiscal year, Academy Sports and Outdoors ecommerce sales increased 14% year over year. Ford added that the retailer is expanding both its offerings and its functionality. The retailer anticipates the channel “to be a tailwind for years to come,” he said.

American Eagle (No. 54)

Mike Mathias, full-time non-executive strategic advisor, said on American Eagle’s Q2 earnings call that both in-store and digital traffic are improving.

“AUR [average unit retail], UPT [units per transaction], AOV [average order value], customer counts, you name it, all going in the right direction with strength across channels, strength across categories, strength across metrics,” he told analysts.

Mathias noted that guidance is “at a flattish result.” In-store sales growth is at the low end of its guidance, whereas digital is stronger, he said.

American Eagle did not break out its ecommerce sales growth in Q2. However, comparable sales — which include ecommerce — increased 6% in American Eagle’s Q2.

Lovesac (No. 409)

In its fiscal Q2 2027, Lovesac omnichannel comparable sales — which include ecommerce — declined 1.9%.

Chief operating officer Mary Fox said Lovesac is making adjustments to its “digital configurations and how we bring Lovesac to life online. We know many of our customers begin their journey online and often purchase in-store.”

She said the furniture retailer is working to advance its digital playbook to bring customers through the purchase funnel.

“As with Q1, we continue to see record levels of web customer satisfaction, demonstrating that our focus in enhancing customer experience and reducing friction will continue to scale,” Fox said.

In addition, Fox noted that Lovesac is rolling out delivery services nationally in its fiscal Q3. It anticipates the rollout will remove friction while building customer relationships, she said.

Macy’s (No. 18)

In its fiscal Q2 206, Macy’s ecommerce contributed to positive comparable sales growth in the quarter. Macy’s digital sales include those from its own brand, Bloomingdale’s and Bluemercury, as well as the Macy’s online marketplace.

CEO Antony Spring called ecommerce “a central component of our omnichannel approach. We’re creating a seamless customer experience across all touchpoints and continue to enhance our digital offerings and connections across channels.”

He noted that the retailer launched its AI-powered conversational assistant, Ask Macy’s, as a starting point for discovery. It’s now expanding that capability to its in-store employees as a support tool. Additionally, Macy’s has launched the same type of AI conversational shopping assistant for Bloomingdale’s.

“This rollout also highlights the power of leveraging enterprise-wide capabilities across Macy’s, Inc. to enhance the customer experience across nameplates,” Spring said.

Chief operating officer and chief financial officer Thomas Edwards said the retailer is seeing “much better engagement” from consumers using the Macy’s and Bloomingdale’s AI shopping assistant. Those consumers have larger carts and higher conversion rates than their counterparts, he said.

Spring noted that “conversion has been more of a challenge” for the retailer. As such, it is spending more time on its product detail pages (PDPs) and the quality of its top-of-funnel marketing, he said. However, Macy’s is also “trying to temper” expectations because some purchases require multiple visits.

“A more expensive mattress or a more expensive diamond or a better quality leather is not an immediate purchase necessarily,” Spring said. “So how do you tease between the immediacy of conversion you’re looking for on every single visit to the site, or to the store, with what may be a browse behavior that’s so important to people becoming and falling in love with your brand and business?”

Shoe Station (No. 568)

In its fiscal Q2 2026, Shoe Station reported double-digit ecommerce growth year over year. Overall Shoe Station ecommerce sales increased 18.8% year over year in its fiscal Q2.

That came as Shoe Station’s comparable store sales — which include ecommerce — declined 2.7% year over year in August. That was “substantial improvement” from a 7.1% decline during Q2, according to CEO Clifton Sifford.

Signet Jewelers (No. 65)

On its fiscal Q2 2027 earnings call, Signet Jewelers CEO James Symancyk referred to the retailer’s website redesigns for the Jared Kay and Zales brands as showing “promising” early results. It has already launched the redesigned sites for the Kay and Jared brands. He said he anticipates the Zales redesign to go live in September.

Symancyk called the new site design “a more modern, intuitive and inspiring shopping experience.”

“You’ll immediately notice better imagery and product presentation that includes more realistic on-model photography to help customers buy with confidence,” Symancyk said. “A simpler navigation structure helps customers get to the right product faster alongside curated experiences that work to connect inspiration directly to product.”

The site changes create a foundation for digital growth, he said. They put Signet Jewelers in a position to create “deeper personalization, agentic discovery and greater omnichannel connectivity.”

“We believe the combination of our marketing playbook and refreshed websites can continue expanding reach and engagement to drive conversion through digital experiences that reinforce brand distinction rather than relying solely on paid traffic,” Symancyk said.

Reformation (No. 343)

In its fiscal Q2 2026, Reformation did not break out its ecommerce sales growth. However, CEO Hali Borenstein celebrated Reformation’s initial public offering (IPO), calling it “a significant milestone and the result of years of work.”

She noted that as a digitally native brand, Reformation combines third-party platforms with proprietary technology that it has designed to drive customer engagement.

Its stores and ecommerce business operate as an integrated, omnichannel ecosystem, she said.

“Both channels have compelling stand-alone economics, but they are meaningfully more productive together,” she said. “Markets with stores grow significantly faster than those without.”

Borenstein noted that Reformation omnichannel customers, who represent 34% of revenue, spend 3.1x more than single-channel customers.

data.title: How Soccer.com's World Cup lift could extend to Cyber 5
data.description:
Months after the 2026 FIFA World Cup final — the event with the biggest impact on Soccer.com sales — the retailer is planning for the Cyber 5.

The five-day period from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday generates traffic increases for the retailer, as do other sales holidays such as Memorial Day, Independence Day and Labor Day.

“Those are meaningful to us as shopping holidays, but for us, it’s more seasonal,” Billy Lalor, director of consumer merchandising for Soccer.com.

He told Digital Commerce 360 that the retailer benefits from increased web traffic around typical shopping holidays, “but they’re not peaks in the way that maybe they are for more general retailers.” Instead, Soccer.com is “just getting over the bell curve of the large peak.” From late July through late August, soccer players are typically getting ready to go back to playing for school or club teams. They gear up for the fall season.

Lalor has noticed that youth-sized fan merchandise tied to the World Cup did not sell through as much as Soccer.com had expected going into the event. He said he wouldn’t characterize those sales as struggling, but he observed they didn’t receive the type of benefit that both adult men’s and women’s products did. Now, he sees youth apparel benefiting from back-to-school season.

When Soccer.com begins preparing for sales peaks

Soccer.com plans its merchandising farther out than six or seven months, according to Lalor. And during a World Cup year, it also had to plan for the sport’s overall growth in the U.S.

So for the Cyber 5, “which is now Cyber Month,” Lalor remarked, Soccer.com already had a plan by the time summer starts.

“There’s nothing particularly significant in terms of product launches around that time that you can put out there to drive a lot of traffic and revenue,” Lalor said.

Instead, consumers are expecting promotions in which they can buy a lot and still save money, he added. And he expects that trend to continue into the 2026 Cyber 5. Part of this year’s challenge will be the accompanying macroeconomic conditions, such as inflation and rising fuel costs.

Lalor noted that macroeconomic conditions have affected Soccer.com’s expenses this year. However, they did not affect the retailer’s supply or timing.

“Flying in the face of that World Cup and soccer momentum,” Lalor said. “We recognize that. The marketplace is going to be as promotional as ever, is my feeling. There’s probably going to still be product left over that people have from the World Cup that they’re going to want to liquidate by the end of the year. So I think there’s going to be a lot of value to be had. We will be promotional within that.”

Soccer.com tries to be “no more promotional than we have to be,” he added. The retailer’s promotions will depend on inventory levels, which Lalor said were “pretty healthy” going into Q4.

Although he doesn’t expect Soccer.com to discount heavily, he expects it to have “some strong offers.” It will be competing not just with the soccer space but with sporting goods retailers at large.

How the Cyber 5 in 2025 affected Soccer.com sales

Lalor said Soccer.com grew sales during the Cyber 5 in 2025 versus 2024. However, he qualified that by noting that Adidas and Puma launched their first wave of World Cup products around that time.

That first wave included products such as home jerseys, the World Cup ball and related assortments.

“So we already got a World Cup bump at holiday,” he said, noticing that there was an overall downward sales trend for Soccer.com during Q4 2025 ahead of those launches.

“And typically, we don’t expect our growth rates outside of that time period to differ much from our growth rate before and after that period,” Lalor added. “We don’t necessarily use it for customer acquisition that much. It depends on how much inventory we need to turn as to how aggressive we need to be or how much we’re going to grow. Margin is always a rate that’s not desirable and not sustainable outside of those five days. So it kind of depends situationally.”

data.title: Target deepens AI push, adding photo search and review insights
data.description:
Target is weaving artificial intelligence (AI) into more everyday shopping tasks, from finding products in a photo to picking up where shoppers left off online.

In a Sept. 8 blog post, the retailer highlighted several AI-powered shopping features it has rolled out since 2025. These include Photo Search, which lets shoppers upload images to find similar products, along with tools that summarize customer reviews, surface past purchases for reordering and bring shoppers back to items they recently viewed.

The update comes as Target puts more leadership behind its AI strategy. The retailer recently appointed Chandhu Nair as its first chief AI officer, effective Aug. 24. During Target’s quarterly earnings call last month, CEO Michael Fiddelke said Nair would help the company “accelerate how we harness the power of AI to create better guest experiences and unlock new capabilities across our business.”

Target is No. 5 in the Top 1000 Database. The market research tool tracks North America’s largest online retailers, ranking them by annual ecommerce sales and more.

Target is also No. 54 in Digital Commerce 360’s all-new AI Rankings. That set of rankings is available in the Top 1000 Pro with AI Database.

Target adds photo search and AI review summaries

Photo Search, the newest of Target’s AI tools, launched in August in the Target app.

Shoppers can tap the camera icon in the search bar, then upload or snap a photo to find similar products “without needing to describe them in words,” the company said.

Meanwhile, AI Review Insights tackles a different shopping task: sorting through dozens or even hundreds of customer reviews online.

Launched in June, the AI tool identifies a product’s commonly discussed attributes and organizes customer feedback into themes, helping shoppers focus on “the information that matters most to their purchase decision,” Target said. For example, the tool could group activewear reviews around topics such as comfort, fit, stretch and breathability.

Target said early results show Review Insights is boosting conversion and add-to-cart activity while reducing what it calls “decision fatigue,” though it did not share specific figures.

Neither of the features is unique to Target. Amazon, for example, has offered photo-based product search through Amazon Lens and AI-generated summaries of customer reviews for several years.

Target leverages AI for repeat purchases

Target is also using AI to simplify repeat purchases. Available through the app’s main navigation, its Buy Again tool surfaces a user’s past purchases, frequently ordered items and relevant deals based on previous shopping behavior. A shopper could pull up a recent grocery order, for example, and quickly add staples such as milk, bread or paper products to a new cart.

After launching Buy Again last year, Target said it has improved the tool’s recommendations and deal selection. The retailer said the experience has delivered “double-digit conversion growth year-over-year, while driving demand in categories like food and beverage.”

Meanwhile, Continue Shopping takes a similar approach to unfinished purchases. Using AI-powered personalization, the feature brings shoppers back to products they recently viewed while also surfacing alternatives and offers across Target’s homepage, My Target and search results. Since launching last fall, Target told Digital Commerce 360 that it is “driving double-digit conversion rates and incremental add-to-carts.”

Target expands AI shopping push

The tools are part of Target’s broader push into AI-driven commerce. On the company’s Q2 earnings call on Aug. 19, chief merchandising officer Cara Sylvester said Target had added AI-powered teacher and college wish lists, along with more personalized content on the app’s home screen.

She said total wish-list creations were up more than 50% from a year earlier, while the number of items added to those lists more than doubled. Conversion across Target’s key back-to-school pages also increased nearly 20%, she said.

Beyond its own app and website, Target is also looking at how shoppers can reach the retailer through outside AI platforms. Fiddelke said Target has partnered with OpenAI, Google Gemini and others as it explores agentic commerce.

Traffic to Target from external AI platforms remains small overall, he said, though its growth rate is more than 3.5 times that of the industry compared with a year ago.

Shipt launches Ask Shipt assistant

Target-owned Shipt is also rolling out its own AI shopping tool, adding another layer to the retailer’s push into conversational commerce. On Sept. 9, the same-day delivery service introduced Ask Shipt in its app and on Shipt.com.

Shipt, which Target acquired in 2017, describes Ask Shipt as an AI assistant that can turn prompts, recipes and meal photos into a shopping cart. Shoppers can describe what they need, and the assistant identifies relevant products and builds a cart. Users can then review, swap or edit its suggestions before checkout.

“Ask Shipt brings people-centric AI directly into the shopping journey, helping members move from inspiration to a personalized cart in moments,” said Katie Stratton, Shipt’s chief growth and strategy officer, in a statement.

Stratton said the tool works across Shipt’s marketplace of more than 100 retailer partners.

The launch comes as Shipt experiments with other conversational entry points. The company said it recently enabled shopping through ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude.

Shipt is also preparing to launch Shared Lists, which will let multiple users contribute to the same shopping list in real time. The feature can then convert the list into a cart with a single click.

data.title: Holidays, made-to-order process drive Polywood sales
data.description:
When Ben Spiegel joined Polywood in 2025, he didn’t anticipate 75% of the outdoor furniture retailer’s sales to come from ecommerce.

He joined the retailer as chief information officer in April 2025 before becoming chief digital officer about a year later. Prior to that, he worked at Health & Beauty and consumer-packaged goods merchants, where sales are largely online. But his expectations for Housewares & Home Furnishings were different.

“I didn’t really expect coming into the category that people would do that,” Spiegel told Digital Commerce 360.” I realized quickly that that’s driven by: you can’t get good products locally — the ones that you want —meaning you go in a showroom and you see something, but it’s not the right color, not the right size, not the right availability. So I’ve been really impressed by our D2C demand and the demand to transact online in this category.”

He identified a what he considered a problem in the category: Mass Merchants and Home Improvement retailers sell a few outdoor furniture products each. Additionally, consumers ordering from “some obscure vendor” wouldn’t know when a product will arrive or what brand it is.

In addition to selling direct-to-consumer (DTC), Polywood sells wholesale and through showrooms.

Polywood’s made-to-order delivery process

“The interesting part about our businesses is it’s vertically integrated, just-in-time manufacturing, meaning you literally click on checkout on Shopify and it triggers lumber being moved to a machine, being extruded, being cut and being shipped to you,” Spiegel said. “So [it’s] this whole idea of one-piece flow versus manufacturing massive amounts of inventory and then trying to push it.”

Upon ordering, Polywood products generally ship out in about five to seven business days, according to Spiegel. He estimated that the retailer keeps a maximum of 5% its inventory on hand.

“We make each piece custom,” Spiegel said. “That means we can give a massive assortment without having to worry about carrying too much inventory, which is a really different approach.”

Polywood’s peak sales periods

As a brand for outdoor products, the vast majority of Polywood’s business — around 80% — occurs between Memorial and Labor days. May alone is a key month for the retailer.

It largely limits itself to sales around those to holidays, but it participates in other promotional periods in different ways. For example, during the Cyber 5, Polywood tends to avoid discounting. However, it might offer faster shipping or limited-time products.

Polywood also sells via Amazon and experience an increase in traffic during the marketplace’s Prime Day event in June this year.

“It was a noticeable spike, and the main issue with this spike is that it was a lot of add to carts and comparison shopping,” Spiegel explained. “Our average purchase price is about $1,600, so we are not as much in the realm of the spontaneous, ‘Hey, I’m emotionally triggered to buy this right now,’ and a lot more in this space of ad planning the purchase.”

In fact, Polywood’s approach to Prime Day is to reduce ad spend. Such promotional periods are when Polywood might sell chairs at the retailer’s lowest price points, he added. That compares to selling dining or deep-seating sets during its busier periods.

“If you’re searching for a dining set and you see Polywood at full price and everybody else at a discount price, it doesn’t really make sense,” Spiegel said.

Polywood also offers sales centered around the 4th of July. This year’s didn’t go as well as 2025, though, he said.

“We see the higher-income level, higher-priced product is not impacted as much,” Spiegel said. “We see the lower-household income/household smaller purchases were dramatically less just due to the soft consumer environment and people’s uncertainty.”

How Polywood prepares for the Cyber 5

Spiegel noted the value of “second-season states” for Polywood during the Cyber 5. He told Digital Commerce 360 that he lives in Florida.

“I don’t go outside until it’s November,” Spiegel said. “So as you think about Black Friday, as you think about that whole season, that is our ‘second season’ with all the southern states. That’s when they do these things, and that’s when we really double down again.”

He explained that the outdoor furniture product space “is always a push sale.” It doesn’t benefit as much from coupon shopping. Rather, Spiegel said, if a consumer is going to buy, then it’s just a matter of when.

To account for that, Polywood focuses on developing the right reach, frequency and context relevance in its ecommerce operations. That involves working with social media influencers and creators to get the retailer into roundups. He gave an example of a roundup called “top five outdoor chairs for your winter yards.” Polywood has more success with that than with the pay-to-click space during the Cyber 5, he said.

Spiegel also noted that purchases windows are about twice as long during the Cyber 5 as compared to its usual sales. Normally, he said, Polywood customers will convert in their first seven days of coming to a retailer’s site. During the Cyber 5 in 2025, he said, that period extended to about 10 to 14 days.

Customers began searching earlier for deals to fill their baskets, he said. Polywood also has two white-label brands, which Spiegel said helps the retailer to see when its customers fill other baskets as well. Once they fill their baskets, he said, they’re waiting to see who will make them an offer first.

“Is there going to be a flash sale? So it becomes this kind of stalking, hunting period for a lot of consumers, which was good for Google and Facebook because we spent more because we have to keep driving them to the site,” Spiegel said. “But it was a lot of just put in your cart and wait, which required us to change our conversion optimization windows and adjust our email and ping and retargeting campaigns to match that.”

He compared the period to tax-refund season, when consumers add to their carts “and they start dream shopping. And then, when it becomes time, they all check out at once.”

data.title: Circle-Tazapay deal aims to accelerate USDC adoption in cross-border B2B payments
data.description:
Circle Internet Group has signed a definitive agreement to acquire Tazapay, a Singapore-based business-to-business (B2B) cross-border payments company, in a deal aimed at accelerating adoption of its USDC stablecoin for global commerce.

Meanwhile, Tazapay brings more than $25 billion in annualized payment volume, banking in over 100 markets, and 60-plus fintech partners. Circle said that infrastructure will help make USDC a faster, more accessible payment rail across Asia-Pacific and emerging markets.

About Circle’s acquisition of Tazapay

The companies expect to close the acquisition in 2027 pending regulatory approvals, including sign-off from the Monetary Authority of Singapore. It deepens a relationship that began in 2025, when Tazapay served as a design partner for Circle Payments Network.

Approximately 60% of Tazapay’s existing transaction volume already involves stablecoins, according to Circle. That underscores how far the Singapore-based platform had already moved toward digital-asset settlement before announcing the deal. Circle is the issuer of USDC, one of the world’s largest dollar-backed stablecoins.

“Stablecoin settlement is becoming core infrastructure in the global economy, and combining USDC with Tazapay’s world-class banking relationships, local payout rails, and institutional customer base will accelerate worldwide USDC adoption,” said Jeremy Allaire, co-founder, CEO and chairman at Circle, in a press release. “Tazapay has been a design partner for Circle Payments Network since 2025 and we share a deep alignment. We are excited to bring the team in-house and work together towards accelerating Circle’s mission.”

Tazapay officials also heralded the move.

“We built Tazapay to make payments faster, remove friction, and streamline dependency on banking rails that don’t operate at the speed of global commerce,” said Rahul Shinghal, co-founder and CEO of Tazapay. “Circle has the dollar infrastructure in USDC and the regulatory standing to take what we’ve built further than we could alone. That’s what makes this the right move and what we’re focused on delivering together.”

Implications of increased USDC stablecoin adoption

Robin Anderson, head of product at Tribe Payments, said the deal shows where stablecoins are gaining traction.

“I don’t think we’re quite there yet on the consumer side — where people wake up and decide they want to pay with USDC,” Anderson said. “But on the payment infrastructure side, it’s a different conversation.”

Anderson noted that Tazapay already has payment rails across more than 100 markets.

“That gives Circle something it would take years to build from scratch — connections into local payment methods, currencies and regulatory environments, as well as an established base of businesses already moving money internationally. It creates a much more direct route for USDC to be used in real-world cross-border commerce,” Anderson said.

He noted stablecoins can help in cross-border payments to solve aspects such as:

  • settlement times
  • restricted banking hours
  • trapped liquidity
  • the number of intermediaries involved in the payment ecosystem

“This fits that use case well,” Anderson said. “However, stablecoins aren’t likely to replace the existing payment system wholesale. Businesses will still need reliable ways to move between stablecoins and local currencies, manage compliance and reach recipients who want to be paid through familiar local methods. Tazapay helps Circle bridge those two worlds.”

He observed that the customer at either end probably won’t know a stablecoin is involved.

“And I’m not sure they need to,” Anderson said. “If the money gets where it needs to go more quickly, predictably, and with fewer steps in between, that’s the part that counts. For me, this deal is another sign that stablecoins are starting to become part of the payment infrastructure rather than something sitting off to the side of it.”
